extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, regulators, consumer advocates, and privacy professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Policy recommendations, background, and proposed regulatory standards in response to the 2017 Equifax data breach, aimed at reforming credit reporting agencies, breach-notification rules, and consumer remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free credit freezes and change default to opt-in
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit reporting agencies (CRAs) should offer free credit 'freezes' and 'thaws,' changing the default for report disclosure to opt-in and establishing a credit freeze for all disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change the default on access to credit reports so disclosures require consumer opt-in; provide free and easy mechanisms for consumers to freeze and thaw reports for specific purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free credit monitoring and easy access to credit history
rubrics_metrics.description: CRAs should provide free monitoring and easy access to credit history so consumers have as much information as possible about the use of their personal data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationalize access to free credit reports (EPIC notes current process is cumbersome). Settlement terms described: consumers can file claims for free credit monitoring or a $125 cash payment; Equifax to provide 6 free credit reports per year; documentation required for higher monetary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic transparency (disclosure of secret scores and algorithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should require mandatory disclosure of secret scores and algorithms used by CRAs; algorithmic transparency is key to accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require disclosure of secret scores, lists, underlying data and the algorithms upon which consumer decisions are based so consumers and regulators can evaluate and remedy harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: National baseline data breach notification standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should set national, baseline data breach notification standards requiring immediate and efficient notification of impacted consumers, regulators, and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal standard should require prompt notification (EPIC suggests companies can notify consumers within 48–72 hours using social media, automated text or e-mail as appropriate) to limit damage from breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandate reasonable data security measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should mandate reasonable data security measures for companies that collect consumers' personal data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt breach notifications are necessary but insufficient; law should require demonstrable, reasonable security practices and permit regulators to enforce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private right of action for consumers affected by breaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers affected by data breaches should have a private right of action; breach of personal data should be sufficient harm to provide a cause of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibit credit reporting agencies and financial institutions from using arbitration agreements to block consumer actions for breach, improper disclosure, or misuse of personal data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA) protections to CRAs
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing data security requirements for consumer-facing financial institutions under GLBA should extend to credit reporting agencies and other companies that sell consumer profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GLBA already provides oversight by regulatory agencies; given CRAs hold highly sensitive data, they should not be exempt from these requirements. Current CFPB authority is limited and should be supplemented with explicit rulemaking authority to set data security guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit use of Social Security numbers by private companies without authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should prohibit the use of the social security number (SSN) in the private sector without explicit legal authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SSNs were never meant to be general-purpose identifiers; limiting private-sector use reduces risk from breaches and identity theft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote privacy-preserving and security technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress and companies should promote and invest in innovative technologies (e.g., differential privacy algorithms, secure two-factor authentication) to minimize collection of personal data and reduce harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt and scale privacy-enhancing techniques and authentication methods; CRAs and other data holders should invest in these defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enact baseline privacy legislation (Consumer Privacy Bill of Rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enact a Consumer Privacy Bill of Rights or baseline privacy legislation that places responsibilities on companies that collect and use personal data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national baseline could harmonize and simplify compliance and help resolve trade disputes with other jurisdictions; legislation should assign clear duties to data collectors and enforcement mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a U.S. Data Protection Agency
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States should establish a Data Protection Agency with authority and personnel to enforce privacy and data security rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current agencies lack sufficient authority and resources; a dedicated agency would provide oversight, enforcement, and capacity-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equifax settlement: consumer remedies and claims process
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the Equifax settlement, consumers can file a claim for free credit monitoring or a $125 cash payment; consumers may seek up to $20,000 for time lost or costs with supporting documentation; Equifax must provide 6 free credit reports per year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit monitoring or $125 cash payment requires no documentation though amounts may be reduced pro rata; documentation is necessary for higher-value claims; consumers should be informed about claim procedures and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely patching of known vulnerabilities and effective scanning
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must promptly apply security patches and ensure vulnerability scans identify vulnerable systems; Equifax failed to patch Apache Struts CVE-2017-5638 in a timely manner despite notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When vendors publish patches (e.g., Apache released a patch March 7, 2017), organizations must act quickly; scans that fail to identify vulnerabilities are inadequate and should be remedied with improved procedures and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use secure, clear breach-notification channels and avoid creating phishing risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Breach notification should use official, secure channels; Equifax's creation of a separate domain (equifaxsecurity2017.com) increased phishing risk and confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications should come from clearly authenticated official domains/accounts, avoid creating easily spoofable domains, and use unambiguous messaging. Do not issue easily-guessable PINs or other insecure authentication tokens in consumer-facing remediation processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent insider trading and improper executive actions around breaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate officers should not trade on nonpublic information related to breaches; Equifax executives were accused of selling stock prior to public announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SEC guidance and enforcement should apply; companies should have policies and controls preventing trading on material nonpublic cybersecurity information.
